claims.claim: Confucius (Kongzi, 'Master Kong') is a historical figure traditionally dated 551-479 BCE; he was born in the region of what is now Shandong province, served as an official in the state of Lu, and late in life turned to teaching.

The Analects (Lunyu) is the key text associated with Confucian traditions: a collection of sayings and dialogues attributed to Confucius and his disciples, assembled over time and reflecting diverse representations of the master.

Core concepts of Confucian traditions include ren (humaneness or benevolence), li (ritual propriety), xiao (filial piety), the five relationships (ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, older and younger siblings, and friends, each carrying mutual duties), and the junzi (the exemplary person or 'gentleman'), a moral ideal open in principle to anyone who cultivates virtue.

Education and self-cultivation are central to Confucian traditions: virtue is developed through study, ritual, and reflection, and the way of the junzi is open to anyone willing to 'work at the roots.'

Scholars debate whether Confucian traditions are a religion, a philosophy, an ethical system, or a civil tradition; Britannica describes Confucianism as sometimes viewed as a philosophy and sometimes as a religion, and OpenStax notes that many consider it more a philosophy or social system than a religion because it focuses on moral wisdom without specific worship or formal objects.

Confucian traditions include state-sponsored ritual and the veneration of ancestors: in imperial China, Confucius himself received ritual offerings in temples in major cities, and ancestral sacrifice was an established practice; Britannica notes there is no deity worshipped in Confucianism, though the worship of ancestors and of Confucius as a sage master and teacher are practiced.

Confucian learning shaped Chinese government for centuries: the Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) revived and popularized the tradition, the classics became the curriculum for training the scholar-officials who staffed the imperial bureaucracy, Confucian learning was central to the imperial examination system, and the examinations were abolished in 1905.

Neo-Confucianism, a Song-period (960-1279) revival that responded to Buddhist and Daoist thought, was anchored by thinkers such as Zhu Xi (1130-1200), whose Four Books curriculum became influential in China, Korea, and Japan.

Confucian traditions interacted with Daoism and Buddhism over centuries, and Confucian values continued to mark government, education, and family life in East Asia; their influence persists in China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, alongside twentieth-century criticism and renewed scholarly and public debate about the tradition's contemporary role.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Confucian traditions constitute a religion.
positions: Britannica: Confucianism is sometimes viewed as a philosophy and sometimes as a religion; it is not an organized religion, yet it entails ancestor reverence and a human-centered religiousness, and there is no deity worshipped in it.

OpenStax: many consider Confucianism more of a philosophy or social system than a religion because it focuses on sharing wisdom about moral practices and does not involve specific worship or formal objects.

Wikipedia: European commentators have debated the classification since the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (Jesuits treated it as an ethical system compatible with Christianity; the Rites Controversy followed), and some scholars describe it as a diffused civil religion in contemporary China.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the classification as an open scholarly debate and describes the positions without adjudicating between them; it also notes that the answer depends on how religion is defined.

positions: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives 'trad. 551-479 BCE' (traditional dates, with the birth year recorded in the Gongyang Commentary).
OpenStax and Britannica give the broader range 'sixth and fifth centuries BCE.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the traditional dates with the 'trad.' qualifier and notes the wider century range, matching how the sources themselves present the dates.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Confucius was the 'founder' of Confucianism.
positions: Britannica: Confucius was not a founder in the sense that the Buddha founded Buddhism or Jesus founded Christianity; he considered himself a transmitter who tried to reanimate the old to attain the new.
Popular usage often credits Confucius with founding Confucianism.
The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that the Chinese term Ru (scholars/specialists in ritual) predates Confucius.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes Confucius as a historical teacher who presented himself as a transmitter of earlier culture, and describes the traditions as a family that developed over time rather than as something founded by one person.

Supports: Confucianism as the way of life propagated by Confucius in the 6th-5th century BCE and followed for more than two millennia; no deity worshipped though veneration of ancestors and of Confucius as a sage master and teacher are practiced; sometimes viewed as a philosophy and sometimes as a religion; not an organized religion yet entailing ancestor reverence and human-centered religiousness; influence on Korea, Japan, and Vietnam; Confucius as transmitter rather than founder; the Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) revival; Confucian values as a source of inspiration in the Sinitic world for over two thousand years.

sourceRecords.title: Confucius (first published 2020, substantive revision May 2, 2024)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: Confucius (trad. 551-479 BCE) as teacher, advisor, editor, philosopher, reformer, and prophet; birth in the domain of Zou in modern Shandong, south of the kingdom of Lu, and an official career in Lu with teaching late in life; the Analects (Lunyu) as the key early collection of sayings and dialogues; virtues of benevolence (ren), righteousness (yi), ritual propriety (li), wisdom (zhi), and trustworthiness (xin); the junzi ('gentleman') as the moral ideal open to all who 'work at the roots'; filial piety (xiao); the five relationships (wulun) formulation; ritual and music as inculcators of values; ancestral sacrifice; ritual offerings to Confucius in temples in all major cities of imperial China; the Han (202 BCE-220 CE) establishment of his authority; Neo-Confucianism as the Song-period (960-1279) post-Buddhist revival, with Zhu Xi (1130-1200) and the Four Books curriculum influential in China, Korea, and Japan; education of scholar-officials in the imperial bureaucracy; twentieth-century criticism and reinterpretation.
